newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyprus talks resume in Switzerland on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks resume in Switzerland on Monday.

text.p: Talks aimed at reuniting Cyprus resume near the Swiss city of Montreux on Monday with both sides damping down optimism despite mounting pressure for a solution that has eluded mediators for decades.

The U.N.-brokered talks between the Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders, Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Denktash, follow a first round last month in Troutbeck, New York, aimed at reuniting the divided island under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Both sides are talking down prospects of much progress at the five-day meeting in a hotel in the Swiss resort of Glion.

Stakes have been raised since the first round with Turkey saying it will move towards partial integration with the northern part of the island and the European Union announcing plans to go ahead with entry talks for Cyprus early next year.

Denktash, who has spent more than three decades at the forefront of the political fight for his community, said on Sunday that his first meeting with Clerides had failed to advance the cause of peace between the rival communities.
"No forward steps were taken on the political scene, and (we can say) it has even gone backwards," he was quoted as saying by Turkish Anatolian news agency during a stopover in Istanbul.

Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence that led to the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force still in Cyprus.
They have been forcibly separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

The Turkish Cypriot state proclaimed in 1983 is recognised only by Ankara, where deputy prime minister Bulent Ecevit, who ordered the invasion as prime minister in 1974, has emerged as a leading hawk on issues involving the breakaway republic.

The New York meeting was the first in three years between the 73-year-old Denktash and 78-year-old Clerides, who have known -- and battled -- each other for nearly half a century, since both were young, London-trained barristers.

In a mini-breakthough last month, the two men agreed to exchange information on the whereabouts of graves presumed to belong to persons missing in hostilities between the two communities and expedite the return of remains to relatives.
On the table in Glion is a U.N.-drafted document calling on the two communities to commit themselves to a sustained process of open-ended, direct negotiations.
But diplomats say a real breakthrough is unlikely before the Greek Cypriot presidential elections in February, when Clerides could lose votes if he goes soft on Denktash.
"I do not know of anything of substance being discussed since Troutbeck," said a senior Greek Cypriot diplomat.
"The U.N. wants to maintain a good climate before the end of the year. Real negotiations will be only after elections."
Added another diplomat close to the talks: "In New York, the two sides agreed that they completely disagree. Unless there is a miracle, Montreux will only confirm that they are wide apart."

Hoping to clear up the problem is the man who brokered peace in Bosnia, U.S. President Bill Clinton's diplomatic troubleshooter Richard Holbrooke who is renowed for his tough but effective and result-oriented negotiating style.

He must bridge positions of both sides that contain elements anathema to the other, like the Greek Cypriot desire for freedom of settlement and the right to own property anywhere in Cyprus and the Turkish Cypriot insistence on sovereign equality.
Denktash on Sunday repeated earlier demands that the Greek Cypriots freeze membership talks with the EU and shelve planned deployment of a Russian-made missile system set for next summer.
"I think, this meeting will be the last one. If no clarity is reached on the topics mentioned above...(the fact) that we can go nowhere will come to light," he declared.
If the talks fail, diplomats fear the east Mediterranean island could end up being more divided than ever.
